name: Nvidia Blackwell-class AI GPUs
what_it_is: Nvidia's newest and fastest AI training chips, the industry standard for building frontier AI models.
used_for: Training and running the largest AI models.
status_detail: Top-end Blackwell chips cannot be sold to China. Reports say the White House refused a cut-down Blackwell variant (B30A) for China; the date of that report is unconfirmed, so treat as likely but not certain.
evidence: Reported B30A would run at roughly half the speed of Nvidia's B300; talks with the administration were public in Aug 2025.

name: Nvidia H200 (licensed sales)
what_it_is: The previous-generation Nvidia Hopper AI chip, still far more powerful than the downgraded chips China was allowed before.
status_detail: US approved case-by-case licenses in Dec 2025/Jan 2026 (25% of revenue to the US government; China volume capped relative to US sales; independent testing). Beijing first blocked imports at customs, then by Aug 2026 reportedly allowed small batches (about 10,000 each to ByteDance and Tencent), with NDRC approval needed and use steered to training. No Sept-Oct 2026 update found.
evidence: US clearance allows up to 100,000 H200s per Chinese buyer; Nvidia reportedly holds about 500,000 H200s in inventory.
contested_note: Supporters say selling older chips keeps China hooked on US tech and funds the US government; critics say it hands China frontier-class training compute and Beijing is using it selectively to build domestic chips.

name: Nvidia H20 (China-specific chip)
what_it_is: A deliberately slowed-down Nvidia AI chip designed to meet US export limits for China.
used_for: Running (inference) and smaller-scale training of AI models.
status_detail: Banned in April 2025, then licensed again in Aug 2025 with a 15% revenue share to the US. Nvidia reportedly wound down H20 production and inventory is limited; H200 has largely superseded it. Current 2026 volumes not confirmed.
evidence: Nvidia agreed to give the US government 15% of H20 China revenue.
contested_note: Critics argue the 15% revenue-share deal turns export controls into a fee and may be unconstitutional as an export tax; supporters call it a pragmatic compromise.

name: AMD MI308 AI GPUs
what_it_is: AMD's cut-down version of its MI300 AI chip made for the China market.
used_for: AI model training and inference in data centers.
status_detail: Needed a license from April 2025 (AMD took an $800M charge); license applications proceeded from July 2025 and AMD said in Dec 2025 it was authorized to ship certain MI308 chips, paying a 15% fee. A more powerful China chip, MI309, reportedly failed the license test. No 2026 shipment data found.
evidence: AMD booked about $800 million in charges when the license requirement hit in April 2025.

name: Chip design software (EDA)
what_it_is: The specialized software engineers use to design and test computer chips; three firms (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA) dominate it.
used_for: Designing every advanced chip, including Chinese AI chips.
status_detail: The US imposed license requirements on EDA sales to China in May 2025, then rescinded them in July 2025 as part of a deal tied to China's rare earth export concessions. No evidence found of reimposition, but the 2026 situation was not directly confirmed.
evidence: Synopsys said the May 29, 2025 restriction letter was rescinded effective immediately.
contested_note: Critics say lifting EDA curbs traded away a key chokepoint for rare earths; the administration framed it as a reciprocal deal.

name: Cadence design tools and IP
what_it_is: Cadence's chip-layout and verification software, used by Chinese designers alongside Synopsys tools.
used_for: Designing AI chips and other processors.
status_detail: Included in the May 2025 EDA license requirement and its July 2025 rescission. Cadence also paid a 2025 US settlement over past China exports (not verified here). Current 2026 status not directly confirmed.
evidence: Commerce told Cadence, Synopsys and Siemens EDA they no longer needed licenses for China sales.

name: Etch and deposition tools (Applied Materials, Lam)
what_it_is: Machines that lay down and carve away ultra-thin layers on silicon wafers to build chips.
used_for: Manufacturing advanced logic and memory chips, including Huawei's AI chips.
status_detail: Advanced-node tools need licenses and Entity List firms (SMIC, Huawei fabs) are largely cut off, while mature-node sales continue. The Sept 2025 Affiliates Rule extended limits to 50%-owned subsidiaries; reportedly suspended until Nov 9, 2026 unless extended. Applied paid a record $252M BIS settlement in Feb 2026 over ion implanters shipped to SMIC via South Korea. Lam (Fremont) is the other major supplier; China is a large share of both firms' revenue.
evidence: Applied expected the Affiliates Rule to cut about $600M from fiscal 2026 sales.
contested_note: Industry argues restrictions hand share to Japanese and Chinese toolmakers; hawks say gaps still let China build advanced chips.

name: Inspection and metrology tools (KLA)
what_it_is: Machines that scan wafers for microscopic defects so fabs can fix problems and raise yield.
used_for: Making advanced chips at usable yields; KLA has near-monopoly share in many inspection steps.
status_detail: Same licensing regime as other US tools; YMTC and other Entity List firms cut off from advanced tools since Dec 2022. One unverified report claims new BIS tool rules in April 2026 hit KLA shares; not confirmed from a primary source.
evidence: KLA shares reportedly fell 4.2% on April 16, 2026 after export-control news (unverified promotional source).

name: Servicing, spare parts and software updates for fab tools
what_it_is: The engineers, replacement parts and software patches that keep already-installed US machines running in Chinese fabs.
used_for: Keeping existing Chinese chip production lines running.
status_detail: US-person support for advanced fabs requires a license since Oct 2022. BIS removed Samsung and SK hynix China fabs from the VEU program effective Dec 31, 2025, with annual licenses reportedly granted for 2026 (not confirmed from a primary source). BIS also penalizes in-China transfers to SMIC (e.g. Exyte, Jan 2026).
evidence: Applied Materials and others saw China service revenue pressured; Exyte paid $1.5M for in-China transfer to SMIC Beijing.

name: High-bandwidth memory (HBM)
what_it_is: Very fast stacked memory placed next to AI chips; AI accelerators need it to perform.
used_for: Pairing with AI GPUs for training and inference.
status_detail: Dec 2024 BIS rule restricts HBM exports to China; Micron says it has not sold HBM there. China's CXMT is reportedly aiming for HBM3 production by late 2026, so this leverage is eroding. Samsung (Korea) is the main supplier Chinese firms stocked up on before the ban.
evidence: Micron reportedly has sold no HBM to China since the Dec 2024 rule.
